in_scope_clauses.summary:
Quality management system and its processes — including the
AS9100D-specific risk-based thinking layered on ISO 9001
§4.4. The QMS shall identify processes, determine their
sequence + interaction, criteria + methods, resources,
responsibilities, and risks + opportunities.

Management review — top management shall review the QMS at
planned intervals to ensure continuing suitability, adequacy,
effectiveness, and alignment with strategic direction. Inputs:
audit results, customer satisfaction, process performance,
product conformity, nonconformities + corrective actions,
monitoring + measurement, supplier performance, risks +
opportunities. (AS9100D uses ISO 9001:2015 numbering §9.3
rather than the older AS9100 Rev C §5.6 numbering.)

Communication — internal and external communications relevant
to the QMS, including communications with customers (especially
regarding product nonconformities and corrective actions) and
regulatory authorities.

Documented information — creation, control, distribution,
access, retrieval, storage, preservation, retention, and
disposition of documented information required by the QMS.
Equivalent to ISO 13485 §4.2.4 / 21 CFR 820.40 in
medical-devices.

Resources — people, infrastructure, work environment,
monitoring + measuring resources, organizational knowledge.
Documented infrastructure qualification covering production
facilities, equipment, software, and tooling.

Operational risk management — aerospace-specific addition to
ISO 9001. Identification, assessment, communication, and
mitigation of risks throughout product realization. Distinct
from product safety risk (which is covered by ARP4761) — this
covers business / operational / supplier / production risk.

Control of externally-provided processes, products and services
(supplier controls) — analogous to ISO 13485 §7.4. Supplier
selection, evaluation, monitoring; flow-down of requirements
including customer + regulatory requirements; counterfeit parts
prevention (per AS5553 when applicable); verification of
received product.

Production and service provision — controlled conditions for
production, including aerospace-specific provisions for FOD
(Foreign Object Debris) prevention, control of equipment +
tooling + software programs, control of work transfers,
validation + control of production processes.

Control of nonconforming output — identification, segregation,
disposition (use-as-is / rework / regrade / scrap / return to
supplier) of nonconforming product. Disposition decisions
require documented authority. Use-as-is + repair dispositions
shall be approved per organizational authority + customer
requirements.

Nonconformity and corrective action — when a nonconformity
occurs, react; evaluate need for action to eliminate cause(s);
implement action; review effectiveness; update risks +
opportunities; make changes to QMS if necessary. Records of
nature of nonconformities, actions taken, and effectiveness.

Type design — drawings, specifications, dimensions, materials,
processes, performance, and any other data necessary to define
the configuration and design features required to show
compliance with the airworthiness requirements. Submitted as
part of the Type Certificate application.

Flight tests — applicant shall conduct all tests necessary to
show compliance with applicable airworthiness requirements,
including flight tests as required. Demonstrate that the
aircraft, aircraft engine, or propeller meets the applicable
airworthiness requirements.

Instructions for Continued Airworthiness (ICA) — holder of
Type Certificate shall furnish at least one set of complete
ICA to each owner of each aircraft incorporating the product
at the time of delivery. ICA include scheduled maintenance,
inspection, troubleshooting, and overhaul instructions.

EASA Type Certificates — type-certification process for civil
aircraft, engines, and propellers per EU Part-21. Includes
design organisation approval (DOA), production organisation
approval (POA), and certification specifications (CS-23,
CS-25, CS-27, CS-29, CS-E, CS-P depending on product type).

Plan for Software Aspects of Certification (PSAC) — the
software certification plan submitted to and agreed with the
certification authority. Defines the software development
lifecycle, processes, tools, standards, and DAL (Design
Assurance Level A through E). Established at SOI (Stage of
Involvement) #1 with the certification authority.

Software Verification Process — the objectives + activities
depend on the software's DAL (A most stringent, E lowest).
Verification covers requirements, design, code, integration,
and tool qualification. DAL-A and DAL-B require independent
verification of specific objectives per Annex A Tables A-3
through A-7.

Software Configuration Management — baseline establishment,
problem reporting, change control, archival + retrieval,
release records, and data control. Configuration items
enumerated and tracked across the software lifecycle.

Software Life Cycle Data — the artifacts produced by the
software lifecycle processes (PSAC, SDP, SVP, SCMP, SQAP,
SRD, SDD, source code, executable object code, SVCP, SCI,
SAS, etc.). All data submitted or available for inspection
by the certification authority.

Stages of Involvement (SOI) with the certification authority —
SOI #1 (Planning Review), SOI #2 (Development Review), SOI #3
(Verification Review), SOI #4 (Final Certification). Each SOI
reviews specific deliverables; SOI #4 issues the Software
Accomplishment Summary (SAS).

Plan for Hardware Aspects of Certification (PHAC) — the
hardware certification plan, analogous to DO-178C's PSAC.
Defines the hardware development lifecycle, processes, tools,
DAL, and the hardware verification + validation approach.

Hardware Validation and Verification Process — covers
requirements validation, implementation verification, design
assurance, and the methods used to demonstrate the hardware
meets its requirements and is suitable for its intended
function at the assigned DAL.

Aircraft system development process — captures functional
requirements, allocates functions to systems, items, and
hardware/software, integrates and verifies. The framework
under which DO-178C software and DO-254 hardware development
live; ARP4754A is the systems context for the lower-level
standards.

Aircraft and system functions allocation — derived
requirements + integration of aircraft-level functions across
systems, items, and external interfaces. Includes derived
safety requirements arising from the ARP4761 safety
assessment process.

Functional Hazard Assessment (FHA) — identifies and classifies
failure conditions of aircraft + system functions according to
severity (Catastrophic / Hazardous / Major / Minor / No Safety
Effect). The FHA's severity classifications drive the DAL
assignments per ARP4754A.

Preliminary Aircraft Safety Assessment (PASA) + Preliminary
System Safety Assessment (PSSA) — top-down analyses identifying
safety requirements for aircraft / system architectures.
Output: derived safety requirements feeding the ARP4754A §6
requirements allocation.

System Safety Assessment (SSA) — verification that the
implemented design meets the safety requirements. Uses Fault
Tree Analysis (FTA), Failure Modes and Effects Analysis
(FMEA), Markov analysis as appropriate. Final SSA report
submitted as part of the certification package.

Common Cause Analysis (CCA) — addresses Zonal Safety Analysis
(ZSA), Particular Risks Analysis (PRA), and Common Mode
Analysis (CMA) to verify that independence claims used in
safety assessment are valid against shared physical zones,
shared resources, and common-mode failures.

First Article Inspection (FAI) — documented complete,
independent, and documented physical and functional
inspection process to verify that prescribed production
methods have produced an acceptable item as specified by
engineering drawings, planning, purchase order, engineering
specifications, and/or other applicable design documents.
Required for new + significantly-changed parts; uses
AS9102 Forms 1/2/3.

Govern function — cultivate and implement a culture of risk
management throughout the organization. Subcategories include
policies and procedures for AI risk management, roles and
responsibilities, accountability structures, diversity and
equity considerations, third-party AI components governance.

Map function — establish the context within which AI risks are
framed. Categorize the AI system, identify intended purposes
and use cases, identify stakeholders, characterize positive
and negative impacts to individuals and society.

Measure function — employ quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-
method tools to assess identified AI risks. Includes test sets,
benchmarks, evaluation methodologies, ongoing monitoring,
tracking of trustworthy characteristics (validity, reliability,
safety, security, accountability, transparency, explainability,
privacy, fairness).

Manage function — prioritize and respond to risks based on the
Measure outputs. Allocate resources to risks based on assessed
impact and likelihood, plan responses, monitor risks over time,
communicate to stakeholders, sunset or decommission as needed.

Risk management system for high-risk AI systems — established,
implemented, documented, and maintained throughout the AI
system lifecycle. Iterative process: identification of known
and reasonably foreseeable risks; estimation and evaluation;
adoption of risk management measures; residual risk evaluation
against acceptability criteria.

Data and data governance for high-risk AI — training,
validation, and testing datasets shall be subject to data
governance and management practices appropriate to the intended
purpose. Datasets shall be relevant, representative, free of
errors, complete; statistical properties documented; bias
examined and mitigated.

Technical documentation for high-risk AI — drawn up before
placing on the market or putting into service, kept up to date.
Demonstrates compliance with Section 2 requirements; provides
authorities with the necessary information to assess
compliance. Content per Annex IV.

Record-keeping / automatic logging — high-risk AI systems shall
automatically record events ("logs") over their lifetime to
ensure traceability appropriate to the intended purpose. Logs
enable identification of situations resulting in risk,
facilitate post-market monitoring, and support reproducibility.

Transparency and provision of information to deployers —
high-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed so their
operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to
interpret outputs and use them appropriately. Accompanied by
instructions for use containing concise, complete, correct,
clear, relevant, accessible information.

Human oversight for high-risk AI — designed and developed so
they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during
use. Oversight measures must enable the natural person to fully
understand system capacities and limitations, remain aware of
automation bias, correctly interpret output, decide not to
use the system, intervene or interrupt operation.

Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity for high-risk AI —
designed to achieve appropriate level of accuracy, robustness,
and cybersecurity, performing consistently throughout lifecycle.
Resilience against errors, faults, inconsistencies; resilience
against unauthorized attempts to alter use, behavior, or
performance.

Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS) — establishment,
implementation, maintenance, and continual improvement of an
AI management system. Parallel structure to ISO 9001 / 13485:
context (§4), leadership (§5), planning (§6), support (§7),
operation (§8), performance evaluation (§9), improvement (§10).
Composes with sector-specific QMS standards as the AI-management
overlay.

Policies for information security — defined, approved by management,
published, communicated to and acknowledged by relevant personnel
and interested parties, and reviewed at planned intervals or when
significant changes occur.

Legal, statutory, regulatory, and contractual requirements relevant
to information security shall be identified, documented, and kept
up to date. The organization's approach to meeting each shall be
defined.

Separation of development, test, and production environments —
including separation of duties where appropriate — to reduce the
risk of unauthorized access or unauthorized changes to the
operational environment.

artifacts.name: Quality policy (AS9100D + ISO 9001:2015 binding)
Standard operating procedure (AS9100D production + documented information)
Internal audit procedure (AS9100D §9.2)
Management review (AS9100D §9.3 / aerospace inputs)
Approved Supplier List (AS9100D §8.4 external provider control)
Supplier evaluation (AS9100D §8.4)
CAPA issue template (AS9100D §10.2)
Nonconformance report (AS9100D §8.7)
Operational risk management file (AS9100D §8.1.4)
Type Certificate Pack Index (14 CFR Part 21 + EASA Part 21)
Plan for Software Aspects of Certification (DO-178C; also covers DO-254 PHAC pending dedicated template)
Software test protocol (DO-178C verification per DAL)
Verification protocol (DO-254 hardware V&V)
System Safety Plan (ARP4754A + ARP4761 framework — covers system development, PASA/PSSA, SSA, CCA)
Functional Hazard Assessment (ARP4761 §3)
First Article Inspection Report (AS9102)
AI System Card / Model Card template
AI Impact Assessment template (EU AI Act + NIST AI RMF aligned)
Software architecture (AI accuracy / robustness / cybersecurity per EU AI Act Art 15)
Technical file index (AI automatic logging per EU AI Act Art 12)
Software release record template (information-security overlay binding)
